%n enūma | ilū | amēlu
#note: See the discussion of the line in OB I.
variants.intertext: Chapter I of the Standard Babylonian @i{Atraḫasīs} is preserved on tablets from the ‘Sippar Library’ (SipNB1), Nineveh (NinNA1 and NinNA2), and a school tablet from Nippur (NipNBSch1). The manuscript of the ‘Sippar Library’, the largest one, has deteriorated considerably over the years. Although it was conserved in 2024, the collation has only recovered some signs of the beginning of the reverse (ll. 75ff.). The various manuscripts, while containing largely the same text, divide it into chapters differently: in fact, the Sippar manuscript’s chapter II begins at line 103 of the Sippar manuscript’ chapter I, resulting in an overlap of nearly 20 lines. This and subsequent chapters of the Standard Babylonian version aim to reconstruct the longer ‘Sippar Library’ version, even when, as in chapter III, no manuscripts of it exist. The ‘Sippar Library’ manuscript of chapter I runs parallel to OB @i{Atramḫasīs} I 1–131.

variants.reconstruction:
%n ilū | nīra || ibnû | tupšikka
#note: See @bib{RN118@184}: “The second line of the opening couplet departs significantly from the OB version, which has @akk{ublū dulla izbilū šupšikka} (I 2). It is easy to see how @akk{ub-lu} and @akk{iz-bi-lu} could be corrupted into @akk{i-lu} and @akk{ib-nu-u₂} by a careless editor, but the substitution of @i{dulla} by @akk{ni-ra} cannot be accounted for in the same way. As already translated, there are two ways of taking @akk{ni-ra}: either it is @i{nīra}, i.e., the first object of @i{ibnû} (the sandwiching of a verb between two accusatives is also found in SB II 90), or it is @i{nēr}, the traditional number of the throng of junior gods. Our preference is marginally for the former, following SB I 41a, where the mutinous gods vow to break the yokes with which they carry their baskets of soil (@i{tupšikku}). However that may be, the remodelling of the couplet shows that, by this scribe at least, the first line was understood as a complete clause. The fact that the Assyrian recension nevertheless gives the incipit as @i{enūma ilū kī amīlī}, “when the gods like men” (@bib{RN2709@533–4}), shows that the scribes of the first millennium were almost as divided as modern scholars by the syntax and meaning of the OB @i{inūma ilū awēlum} (see above, fn. 1).”

variants.reconstruction:
%n šūt (|) āni | īlû | šamêšu
#note: See @bib{RN118@184-185}: “17–18. The word @i{šamêšu} replaces OB @i{šamêša} < @i{šamāʾ-iša}(@i{m}) (or < @i{šamê-ša}(@i{m}): see @bib{RN435@148}). If correctly read, the word @i{apsâšu}, replacing [@i{ana a}]@i{psî}, is coined by analogy with @i{šamêšu}, although we might have expected @i{apsîša}, as in Abi-ešuḫ’s Love Lyrics (@bib{lambert1966divine@54}, 4: @akk{ap-si-ša}). Compare @akk{u₂-ri-id-ma ap-si-šu-um} in YBC.2394 viii 32′ (@bib{FostGeo2020@48}).

variants.reconstruction:
%n irtēqū | ... || šūt (|) šamāmī
#note: Concerning the lines 19-20 see @bib{RN118@185}: “The OB couplet probably reads @akk{[ir-te-qu₂ (i-lu) šu]-u₂-u[t š]a-ma-i | [du-ul-lam u₂-ša]-a[z-bi]-lu {d}i-gi-gi} (for I. 20 see already @bib{RN2009@160}). In our l. 19 the sequence of signs @akk{e-x-x} suggests @i{Enukkū}, the Anunnaki, but the traces are not secure. If we have read I. 20 correctly, the verb is no longer causative and the object Igigi has become the subject, @i{šūt Ellil}.”

variants.reconstruction:
%n miṭrāt (|) ilī || napašti (|) māti
#note: See @bib{RN118@185}: “This line, a repetition of I. 22 inadvertently omitted at the time of writing, and appended on the left edge in the conventional manner, is noteworthy for the spelling @akk{na-pa-aš₂-ti}, against @akk{na-piš-ti} in I. 22. Unless we account it a simple error, this must be explained as an archaism, for @i{napaštum} occurs in Old Akkadian, and once at Mari (ARM I 1, rev. 11', time of Yahdun-Līm). It is usual in Old Assyrian, of course.”

variants.reconstruction:
%n pānīša? | ... | idiqlat
#note: Collation reveals that the Tigris is created “first” or “on the front side” (of the land?) and the Euphrates “afterwards” or “on the back side”. When both rivers are mentioned, the Tigris normally appears before the Euphrates; some texts describe them as being “to the right” and “to the left,” respectively (@bib{blaschke2018euphrat@229}).
